{"name": "Mars Crust", "subtitle": "", "body": "(Note: toggle off the crust layer in the legend to better see the interior structure.)

Mars has a crust, which is the outermost solid shell. Interestingly, recent findings from marsquakes
suggest that the Martian crust is significantly thicker than Earth's, perhaps averaging around 70 kilometers
(43 miles) or even thicker in some areas.

Today, Mars doesn't have a planet-wide magnetosphere generated by a global magnetic field. However, the Mars Global
Surveyor mission discovered strong, localized magnetic fields embedded in certain regions of the Martian crust,
particularly in the ancient southern highlands. These are remnants of the early global field. These localized fields
can create small, localized magnetospheres, but they don't provide planet-wide protection like Earth's magnetosphere."}

text:
Mars Crust
(Note: toggle off the crust layer in the legend to better see the interior structure.)

Mars has a crust, which is the outermost solid shell. Interestingly, recent findings from marsquakes
suggest that the Martian crust is significantly thicker than Earth's, perhaps averaging around 70 kilometers
(43 miles) or even thicker in some areas.

Today, Mars doesn't have a planet-wide magnetosphere generated by a global magnetic field. However, the Mars Global
Surveyor mission discovered strong, localized magnetic fields embedded in certain regions of the Martian crust,
particularly in the ancient southern highlands. These are remnants of the early global field. These localized fields
can create small, localized magnetospheres, but they don't provide planet-wide protection like Earth's magnetosphere.

{"name": "Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide", "subtitle": "", "body": "(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).

* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere."}

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

Scientists often divide the Martian atmosphere into layers based on temperature profiles, similar to Earth's
atmosphere, although some layers are absent or behave differently:
* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.

lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

* Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, extending from the surface up to about 40-50 kilometers (25-31 miles).
Most of Mars' weather, like dust storms and convection, occurs here. The temperature generally decreases with altitude.
* Mesosphere: Above the troposphere, extending from about 50 to 100 kilometers (31 to 62 miles). This layer has the
lowest temperatures in the Martian atmosphere as carbon dioxide efficiently radiates heat into space. Carbon dioxide
ice clouds have even been observed in the Martian mesosphere.
* Thermosphere: Above the mesosphere, starting around 100 kilometers (62 miles) and extending to about 200 kilometers
(124 miles). This layer is heated by extreme ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and temperatures increase with
altitude. However, it's still much colder than Earth's thermosphere.

Atmosphere: Mars has a thin atmosphere, much less dense than Earth's. It's primarily composed of carbon dioxide
(about 95%), with small amounts of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.

thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form."}

data.name: Mars: Upper Atmosphere
text:
Upper Atmosphere: Like Earth, Mars has upper atmospheric layers, including an ionosphere and exosphere, where
the atmosphere becomes very thin and interacts with solar radiation and the solar wind.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

Exosphere: This is the outermost layer, starting above the thermosphere (around 200 km/124 miles) and gradually
thinning out into space. Atoms and molecules here are so far apart that they can escape the planet's gravity.

Interaction with Solar Wind: Without a global magnetosphere, the Martian atmosphere is directly exposed to the
solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. This interaction is believed to have played a significant
role in stripping away much of Mars' early, potentially thicker atmosphere and contributing to the loss of liquid
water on the surface. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a stratosphere. On Earth, the stratosphere is characterized by a
temperature inversion due to the absorption of ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer. Mars has a very thin
atmosphere and no significant ozone layer, so this distinct layer doesn't form.

_encyclopedia.Psyche:
Horizons:-255. JPL: "BACKGROUND:
Psyche is a NASA Discovery-class mission to map the surface and characterize
the composition of '16 Psyche', an elongated 280-km diameter metal-rich
asteroid located in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. This
is the first mission to a metal-rich asteroid.

Psyche was launched Oct 13, 2023 @ 14:19:43 UTC on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy
from Kennedy Space Center, LC-39A.  Stage separation occurred 62 minutes
after launch at 15:21 UTC.

A gravity-assist flyby of Mars will occur in May 2026 at an altitude of
3000-4400 km above the surface, exact details depending on launch date.

The arrival phase ends June 26, 2029.
The asteroid's gravity will capture the spacecraft into orbit in late July
2029 and the two-year prime mission will begin in August. Psyche will
successively lower its orbit over the span of a year, eventually coming
as close as 75-km from the asteroid's surface.

_encyclopedia.Phobos:
Horizons: 401. The larger and closer of Mars's two moons, spiraling inward towards Mars.
Phobos is the larger and innermost of the two Martian satellites. It is a heavily cratered, low-density object that orbits closer 
to its parent planet than any other moon in the solar system.
Dimensions: It is a non-spherical, "triaxial" ellipsoid measuring approximately 26.0 x 22.8 x 18.2 km. Mean Radius: 11.1 km.
Mass: Approximately 1.0659 10^16 kg.
Density: It has a very low mean density of about 1.876 g/cm³, suggesting a porous "rubble pile" composition or a mix of rock and ice.
Surface Gravity: Extremely weak at 0.0057 m/s², meaning a person could easily jump off the surface into orbit.
Proximity: It orbits Mars at a mean distance of only 9,376 km from the planet's center (about 6,000 km from the surface).
Orbital Period: It completes one revolution every 7 hours and 39 minutes, meaning it orbits Mars three times in a single Martian day.
Tidal Locking: It is synchronously rotating, meaning the same face always points toward Mars.
Apparent Motion: Because it orbits faster than Mars rotates, it is the only moon that appears to rise in the West and set in the East.
Stickney Crater: Its most prominent feature is a massive impact crater nearly 9 km wide—large enough that the impact almost shattered the moon.
Orbital Decay: Phobos is below the "synchronous orbit" radius. Tidal forces are slowly dragging it closer to Mars at a rate of about 2 meters 
every 100 years. In roughly 30 to 50 million years, Phobos will either crash into Mars or be ripped apart by gravity to form a planetary ring.
Dust Rings: The moon is a source of seasonal dust rings around Mars as micrometeoroid impacts kick material off its surface.
Discovery: Found by Asaph Hall on August 18, 1877, just six days after he discovered the outer moon, Deimos.
Origin Theories: Scientists are still debating if Phobos is a captured carbonaceous asteroid from the main belt or formed from Martian impact debris.
Psyche Mission: On May 15, 2026 19:51 UTC the Psyche spacecraft will pass within 1,151 km of this moon.
